# Subsequence Matching and LCS with Segment Number Constraints

**Abstract**

The _longest common subsequence_ (_LCS_) is a fundamental problem in string processing which has numerous algorithmic studies, extensions, and applications. A sequence _u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>f</sub>_ of _f_ strings is said to be an (_f_-)segmentation of a string _P_ if \(P=u_1\cdots u_f\). Li et al. [BIBM 2022] proposed a new variant of the LCS problem for given strings _T_<sub>1</sub>_,T_<sub>2</sub> and an integer _f_, which we hereby call the segmental LCS problem (SegLCS), of finding (the length of) a longest string _P_ that has an _f_-segmentation which can be embedded into both _T_<sub>1</sub> and _T_<sub>2</sub>. Li et al. [IJTCS- FAW 2024] gave a dynamic programming solution that solves SegLCS in _O(fn_<sub>1</sub>_n_<sub>2</sub>) time with _O(fn_<sub>1</sub>+_n_<sub>2</sub>) space, where _n_<sub>1</sub>=|_T_<sub>1</sub>|, _n_<sub>2</sub>=|_T_<sub>2</sub>|, and \(n_1\le n_2\). Recently, Banerjee et al. [ESA 2024] presented an algorithm which, for a constant \(f\ge 3\), solves SegLCS in \(\tilde{O}((n_1n_2)^{1-(1/3)f-2})\) time<sup>1</sup>. In this paper, we deal with SegLCS as well as the problem of segmental subsequence pattern matching, SegE, that asks to determine whether a pattern _P_ of length _m_ has an _f_- segmentation that can be embedded into a text _T_ of length _n_. When _f_=1, this is equivalent to substring matching, and when _f_=|_P_|, this is equivalent to subsequence matching. Our focus in this article is the case of general values of _f_, and our main contributions are threefold:

(1) \(O((mn)^{1-\epsilon})\)-time conditional lower bound for SegE under the strong exponential-time hypothesis (SETH), for any constant \(\epsilon>0\).

(2) _O(mn_)-time algorithm for SegE.

(3) \(O(fn_2(n_1-\ell+1))\)-time algorithm for SegLCS where \(\ell\) is the solution length.

## 1 Introduction

The _longest common subsequence_ (_LCS_) is a fundamental problem in string processing which has numerous algorithmic studies, extensions, and applications. Li et al. [13] proposed a new variant of the LCS problem for given string _T_<sub>1</sub>_,T_<sub>2</sub> and integer _f_, which we hereby call the _segmental LCS_ problem (SegLCS). A sequence _u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>f</sub>_ of _f_ strings is said to be an (_f_-)segmentation of a string _P_ if \(P=u_1\cdots u_f\). SegLCS asks to find (the length of) a longest string _P_ that has an _f_-segmentation which can be embedded into both _T_<sub>1</sub> and _T_<sub>2</sub>. Throughout this paper, we assume \(n_1=|T_1|\le n_2=|T_2|\) without loss of generality. Li et al. [12] gave a dynamic programming solution that solves SegLCS in _O(fn_<sub>1</sub>_n_<sub>2</sub>) time with _O(fn_<sub>1</sub>+_n_<sub>2</sub>) space. Recently, Banerjee et al. [1] presented an algorithm which, for a constant \(f\ge 3\), solves SegLCS in \(\tilde{O}((n_1n_2)^{1-(1/3)f-2})\) time. April 8, 2025 DRAFT

The framework of Banerjee et al. \[1\] is general enough to solve other related problems, including the segmental version of the _Episode Subsequence Matching_ in \(\tilde{O}((n_1n_2)^{1-(1/3)^{f-2}})\) time for a constant \(f\ge 3\).

In this paper, we deal with the general case where _f_ is not necessarily a constant, and our focus is to analyze the complexities of these problems. Namely, we consider SegLCS as well as the decision version of the segmental subsequence pattern matching, SegE, that asks to determine whether _P_ of length _m_ has an _f_-segmentation that can be embedded into a text _T_ of length _n_. When _f_=1, this is equivalent to the standard substring pattern matching, and when _f_=|_P_|, this is equivalent to the standard subsequence pattern matching, both of which admit linear-time solutions.

Our focus in this article is the case of general values of _f_. The main contributions of this paper are threefold:

(1) \(O((mn)^{1-\epsilon})\)-time conditional lower bound for SegE (Problem 1) under the strong exponential- time hypothesis (SETH), for any constant \(\epsilon>0\).<tbc>

(2) _O(mn_)-time algorithm for SegE (Problem 1).<tbc>

(3) \(O(fn_2(n_1-\ell+1))\)-time algorithm for SegLCS (Problem 3) where \(\ell\) denotes the length of the solution.

Result (2) gives a matching upper bound with the conditional lower bound of Result (1) for SegE. Also, this algorithm works in _O(mn_) time independently of the value of a given _f_, and thus, it is faster than applying the _O(fmn_)-time SegLCS solution by Li et al. \[12\] to SegE. Our algorithm \(O(fn_2(n_1-\ell+1))\)-time of Result (3) is based on the approach by Banerjee et al. \[1\] and Nakatsu et al.’s LCS algorithm \[15\], which is at least as efficient as the _O(fn_<sub>1</sub>_n_<sub>2</sub>)-time solution by Li et al. \[12\], and can be faster when the solution is sufficiently long. In particular, when \(n_1-\ell=O(1)\), our algorithm runs in _O(fn_<sub>2</sub>) time.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: We give basic notions and define our problems in Section 2. In Section 3 we present our lower bound for SegE, and in Section 4 we give an algorithm for SegE running in _O(mn_) time. Section 4.2 shows that SegE can be solved in _O(m+n_) time by a KMP-based algorithm if _f_=2. Section 5 is devoted for our \(O(fn_2(n_1-\ell+1))\)-time algorithm for SegLCS. We conclude in Section 6.

## 2 Preliminaries

Let \(\Sigma\) be an alphabet. An element of \(\Sigma\) is called a character. An element of \(\Sigma^\star\) is called a string. The empty string \(\lambda\) is the string of length 0. For any strings _u_ and _v_, we denote by \(u\cdot v\) the concatenation of the strings. We often denote \(uv=u\cdot v\) if there is no confusion. For any string _u_ and a positive integer _e_, we define \(u^0=\lambda\) and _u<sup>e</sup>=uu_<sup>_e_-1</sup>. For a string _T_, the length of _T_ is denoted by |_T_|. If _T=xyz_ holds for some strings \(x,y,z\in\Sigma^\star\), then _x_, _y_, and _z_ are called a prefix, a factor, a suffix of _T_, respectively. For an integer _i_ with \(1\le i\le|T|\), the _i_th character of _T_ is denoted by _T_\[_i_\]. For integers _i,j_ with \(1\le i\le j\le|T|\), the factor of _T_ starting at position _i_ and ending at position _j_ is denoted by _T_\[_i..j_\]. For two strings _S_ and _T_, we denote by lcsuf(_S,T_) the length of longest common suffix of _S_ and _T_.

A sequence (_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>f</sub>_) of _f_ strings is called an _(f-)segmentation_ of its concatenation _u_<sub>1</sub>_...u<sub>f</sub>_, where each _u<sub>i</sub>_ is said to be a _segment_ of the _f_-segmentation. We say that a segmentation (_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>f</sub>_) of a string _P_ can be _embedded_ to another string _T_ if there exists a sequence (_p,g_<sub>1</sub>_,...,g_<sub>_f_-1</sub>_,s_) of _f_+1 (possibly empty) strings such that \(T=p\cdot u_1\cdot g_1\cdot u_2\cdot g_2\cdots g_{f-2}\cdot u_{f-1}\cdot g_{f-1}\cdot u_f\cdot s\). Each _g<sub>i</sub>_ is said to be a _gap_ in the embedding. We say that _P_ is an _f-segmental subsequence_ of a string _T_ if<tbc>

there exists an _f_-segmentation (_u_1_,...,uf_) of _P_ that can be embedded to _T_. The set of _f_-segmental subsequences of _T_ is denoted by \(SubSeq^{\le f}(T)\). Any element of \(SubSeq(T)=\bigcup_SubSeq^{\le f}(T)\) is called a _subsequence_. We consider the following decision problem: **Problem 1** (SegE)**.** Given strings _T_ and _P_ and a positive integer _f_, decide whether \(P\in SubSeq^{\le f}(T)\). Note that since each gap _gi_ in an embedding can be the empty string, SegE asks if _P_ has a segmentation with at most _f_ segments that can be embedded into _T_. The following problem asks the minimum number of segments with which _P_ can be embedded into _T_: **Problem 2** (MinSegE)**.** Given strings _T_ and _P_, find the smallest positive integer _f_ such that \(P\in SubSeq^{\le f}(T)\) if it exists, and return _nil_ otherwise. We also consider the segmental version of the _longest common subsequence_ (_LCS_) problem, which we call SegLCS2. A pattern _P_ is said to be an _f-segmental common subsequence_ (_f-SegCS_) of two strings _T_1 and _T_2 if _P_ has a segmentation (_u_1_,...,uf_) of size _f_ that can be embedded to both _T_1 and _T_2. We denote by slcs(_S,T,f_) the length of a longest _f_-SegCS of _S_ and _T_. **Problem 3** (SegLCS)**.** Given strings _T_1_,T_2, and a positive integer _f_, compute slcs(_T_1_,T_2_,f_). ## 3 \(O\big(\big(mn\big)^{1-\epsilon}\big)\)-time Conditional Lower Bound for SegE In this section, we present a lower bound for SegE such that there is no strongly sub-quadratic solution exists unless the famous _strong exponential-time hypothesis_ (_SETH_) fails. **Problem 4** (_k_-SAT problem)**.** Given a propositional logic formula of conjunctive normal form which has at most _k_ literals in each clause, decide whether there exists an interpretation that satisfies the input formula. **Conjecture 1** (The Strong Exponential-Time Hypothesis; SETH)**.**

## 4 Algorithms for SegE In this section, we give a matching upper bound for SegE. We do so by presenting an algorithm for the function version of the problem, MinSegE, running in _O(mn_) time, where _m_=|_P_| and _n_=|_T_|. ### 4.1 _O(mn_)-time Algorithm for general \(f\ge 1\) Shapira and Storer considered Problem 2 in the context of _generalized edit distance problems_ with block deletions, and proposed an _O(mn_2)-time algorithm (Algorithm 2 of \[16\]). However, there is a room for improvements in their algorithm, e.g., employing a standard memorization technique in function during\_deletion appears to provide _n_ times speedup. On the other hand, Problem 2 can be seen as a special case of the global alignment with _affine gap penalty_, where the _gap open penalty_ equals 1, the _gap extension penalty_ equals 0, and any gap in _P_ is prohibited. Our algorithm below is inspired by alignment algorithms with affine gap penalties \[17, 8, 9, 3, 7\]. **Theorem 3.** _The problem MinSegE can be solved in O_(|_T_||_P_|) _time._ _Proof._ By definition of \(SubSeq^{\le f}(T)\), if \(P\in SubSeq^{\le f}(T)\) holds, then _P_ is obtained by deleting (1) a (possibly empty) prefix of _T_, (2) a (possibly empty) suffix of _T_, and (3) at most _f_-1 non-empty factors of _T_ that are neither prefix nor suffix from _T_. The smallest such number _f_ can be computed as _f=d_+1, where _d_ is the minimum number of _edit operations_ to obtain _P_ from _T_ by (i) deleting a prefix _y_ that changes _yx_ into _x_ with cost 0, (ii) deleting a suffix _y_ that changes _xy_ into _x_ with cost 0, and (iii) deleting a string _y_ that changes _xyz_ into _xz_ with cost 1, where \(x,y,z\in\Sigma^+\). Thus, the standard dynamic programming algorithm \[18\] can be applied, by designing the cost function properly as follows. Both the _substitution_ and _insertion_ operations cost \(\infty\) to be prohibited. The _block deletion_ of _y_ costs 0 if _y_ is either prefix or suffix, and costs 1 otherwise. Precisely, we can compute the smallest cost _d_ as follows. We utilize two tables _D_ and _E_ of size \(n\times m\), where _n_=|_T_| and _m_=|_P_|. The value _D_\[_i,j_\] indicates the edit distance between _T_\[1.._i_\] and _P_\[1.._j_\] such that the last operation is a character deletion of _T_, and the value _E_\[_i,j_\] gives the edit distance between _T_\[1.._i_\] and _P_\[1.._j_\], where _D_ and _E_ both assume that the deletion of a suffix of _T_ costs 1 instead of 0. These two tables are linked by the following recurrence relations. \(D[i,0]=E[i,0]=0\text{for}0\le i\le n,\)
\(D[0,j]=E[0,j]=\infty\text{for}1\le j\le m,\)
\(D[i,j]=min\{D[i-1,j],E[i-1,j]+1\},\text{and}\)
\(E[i,j]=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } min\{E[i-1,j-1],D[i,j]\} & (T[i]=P[j]) \\ D[i,j] & (T[i]\neq P[j]) \end{array}\right.\)
\(\text{for}1\le i\le n\text{and}0\le j\le m.\) Note that, in the third equation, the "+1" term indicates the cost to begin a block deletion. The smallest cost _d_ is given by \(min_{1\le i\le n}\{E[i,m]\}\), because we allow to delete a suffix of _T_ with cost 0. If \(d=\infty\), it means that \(P\notin SubSeq(T)\). The total running time is _O_(|_T_||_P_|). ### 4.2 _O(m+n_)-time Algorithm for \(f\le 2\) We show a faster algorithm for a special case of SegE where the segmentation number _f_ is at most two. If _f_=1, the problem is nothing more than the standard exact pattern matching, so that it can be solved in _O_(|_T_|+|_P_|) time with _O_(1) space \[6, 4\]. Here, we focus on the case where _f_=2.

**Theorem 4.** _The problem SegE with input f_=2 _can be decided in O_(|_T_|+|_P_|) _time with O_(|_P_|) _space._ For a text _T_ of length _n_ and a pattern _P_ of length _m_, we define three arrays of size _n_ as follows: \(lpf[i]=max\{l|P[1..l]=T[i-l+1..i]\},\)
\(lsf[i]=max\{l|P[m-l+1..m]=T[i..i+l-1]\},\)
\(llpf[i]=max\{lpf[j]|j\le i\},\text{for each}1\le i\le n.\) The value _lpf_\[_i_\] (resp. _lsf_\[_i_\]) represents the length of the longest prefix (resp. suffix) of _P_, whose occurrence ends (resp. begins) at position _i_ in _T_. 1 shows an example. **Theorem 5.** _Given strings T_<sub>1</sub> _and T_<sub>2</sub> _with_ \(|T_1|\le|T_2|\) _over a linearly sortable alphabet, and integer f, the problem SegLCS can be solved in_ \(O(f|T_2|(|T_1|-\ell+1))\) _time using_ \(O(\ell(|T_1|-\frac{\ell}{f}+1))\) _space, where_ \(\ell=\mathsf{slcs}(T_1,T_2,f)\).

The basic idea of our algorithm is to combine the ideas from Banerjee et al.’s algorithm \[1\] for the SegLCS problem and the method of Nakatsu et al. \[15\] for the (standard) LCS problem. Banerjee et al. \[1\] considered a function<sup>3</sup> _C_ such that _C(i,j,h_)=slcs(_T_<sub>1</sub>\[1_..i_\]_,T_<sub>2</sub>\[1_..j_\]_,h_) for \(1\le i\le n_1\), \(1\le j\le n_2\), and \(1\le h\le f\). They showed that _C_ can be computed by the following recurrence:

\(C(i,j,h)=max\{C(i,j-1,h),C(i-1,j,h),Z\},\)

where _Z=x+C(i-x,j-x,h_-1) and _x_=lcsuf(_T_<sub>1</sub>\[1_..i_\]_,T_<sub>2</sub>\[1_..j_\]). This recurrence provides an _O(fn_<sub>1</sub>_n_<sub>2</sub>)-time algorithm since lcsuf(_T_<sub>1</sub>\[1_..i_\]_,T_<sub>2</sub>\[1_..j_\]) can be computed in _O_(1) time after _O(n_<sub>1</sub>+_n_<sub>2</sub>)- time preprocessing by using a _lowest common ancestor_ query \[10\] on the _suffix tree_ \[19, 5\] of the reversal of _T_<sub>1</sub>_T_<sub>2</sub>. We further speed up the solution by combining Nakatsu et al.’s method.

Our algorithm maintains a three-dimensional table. Let _L(i,s,h_) be the length _j_ of the shortest prefix _T_<sub>2</sub>\[1_..j_\] of _T_<sub>2</sub> satisfying slcs(_T_<sub>1</sub>\[1_..i_\]_,T_<sub>2</sub>\[1_..j_\]_,h_)=_s_. If there are no such prefixes, let \(L(i,s,h)=\infty\). Then, we have

\(\mathsf{slcs}(T_1,T_2,f)=max\{s|L(i,s,f)\neq\infty\text{for some}i\}.\)

Our goal is to compute the table _L_ by dynamic programming, but as we will see later, we do not have to completely fill the table to obtain the value slcs(_T_<sub>1</sub>_,T_<sub>2</sub>_,f_).

We have the following inequalities by definition.

\(L(i,s,h)\le L(i-1,s,h)\) (1)

\(L(i,s,h)>L(i-1,s-1,h)\) (2)

Also, we obtain the following lemmas.

**Lemma 2.** _For any i,j,s, and h, if_ \(j\ge L(i-x,s-x,h-1)+x\) _holds where x_=lcsuf(_T_<sub>1</sub>\[1_..i_\]_,T_<sub>2</sub>\[1_..j_\])_, then_ \(L(i,s,h)\le j\) _holds._

_Proof._ Since \(j-x\ge L(i-x,s-x,h-1)\), _T_<sub>1</sub>\[1_..i-x_\] and _T_<sub>2</sub>\[1_..j-x_\] have (_h_-1)-SegCS of length _s-x_. Thus, _T_<sub>1</sub>\[1_..i_\] and _T_<sub>2</sub>\[1_..j_\] have _h_-SegCS of length _s_ since _x_=lcsuf(_T_<sub>1</sub>\[1_..i_\]_,T_<sub>2</sub>\[1_..j_\]). Therefore, \(L(i,s,h)\le j\) holds.

The next lemma states that, intuitively, a right-aligned embedding of a string into _S_ and _T_ can be transformed into another embedding while maximizing the length of the rightmost segment without increasing the segmentation size.

**Lemma 3.** _Suppose p_=(_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>h</sub>_) _is an h-segmentation of a string of length s_=|_u_<sub>1</sub>_...u<sub>h</sub>_| _such that p can be embedded to both of S and T and the last segment u<sub>h</sub> is a common suffix of S and T. Then, there is an h-segmentation_ \(p'=(u'_1,\dots,u'_h)\) _of a string of length s that can be embedded to both S and T such that_ \(|u'_h|=min\{\mathsf{lcsuf}(S,T),s\}\).

_Proof._ Let \(\ell=\mathsf{lcsuf}(S,T)\). If \(\ell\ge s\), then the _h_-segmentation \((\varepsilon,\dots,\varepsilon,S[|S|-s+1,|S|])\) of _S_\[|_S_|-_s_+1,|_S_|\]=_T_\[|_T_|-_s_+1.|_T_|\] has the desired property. If \(\ell<s\), let _j_ be the integer such that |_u_<sub>1</sub>_...u_<sub>_j_-1</sub>|_\<s_-\(\ell\le|u_1\dots u_j|\). Such _j_ always exists. Also, _j\<h_ holds since \(|u_h|\le\ell\). Let _v_ be the prefix of _u<sub>j</sub>_ such that \(|u_1\dots u_{j-1}v|=s-\ell\). Let \(u'_h=S[|S|-\ell+1,|S|]\). Then, the sequence of _h_ segments \((u_1,\dots,u_{j-1},v,\varepsilon,\dots,\varepsilon,u'_h)\) has the desired property.

## 6 Conclusions and discussions

In this paper, we have studied two basic problems concerning _f_-segmental subsequences: the pattern matching problem and the LCS problem. Concerning the former, we have presented a quadratic- time algorithm for general \(f\ge 1\) and a linear-time algorithm for \(f\le 2\). We also argued that the quadratic time complexity is unavoidable under the strong exponential-time hypothesis. The latter problem has already been studied in the literature The _f_-segmental LCS problem and its variants<tbc>

<tbc>have already been studied in the literature \[13, 12, 1\]. Our algorithm runs faster than theirs when the solution is long.

Studying mathematical and computational properties of subsequences formed by a limited number of segments is relatively a new topic. Below, we raise a few open questions related to the properties of _f_-segmental subsequences among many possible research directions.

• Is it possible to decide whether \(P\in SubSeq^{\le f}(T)\) more efficiently than _O(mn_) time for general _f_? Our proof of the conditional lower bound uses \(f\in\Theta(m)\), while Banerjee et al. \[1\] showed that it can be determined in \(\tilde{O}((n_1n_2)^{1-(1/3)^{f-2}})\) time for a \(constantf\ge 3\). For example, would an _O(fn_)-time algorithm exist?<tbc>

• Does the conditional lower bound on the time complexity of SegE (Theorem 2) hold for binary alphabets? We are somewhat optimistic on this question. Using a similar technique by Bille et al. \[2, Theorem 1\], one may be able to reduce the alphabet size, where we might need to use a direct reduction from the orthogonal vector problem, from which Bille et al. have shown the conditional lower bound on episode matching.<tbc>

• Can we enumerate "minimal occurrences" of _P_ in _T_ as subsequences with at most _f_ segments as in the episode matching, for non-constant _f_? Banerjee et al. \[1\] showed it is possible to find one of such occurrences in \(\tilde{O}((n_1n_2)^{1-(1/3)^{f-2}})\) time for a \(constantf\ge 3\).<tbc>

• Can we bound the size of _subsequence DFAs_ for SegE? Can we efficiently construct such DFAs? One can see that a DFA accepting exactly \(SubSeq^{\le f}(T)\) requires \(\Theta(f|T|)\) states when _T_=(`ab`)_<sup>n</sup>_ and \(f\le n/2\), but we do not know if there are any texts for which DFAs require more states than \(\Theta(f|T|)\).<tbc>

• Is it possible to efficiently construct an indexing structure for _T_ on which one can efficiently decide whether _P_ is an _f_-segmental subsequence of _T_? The above observation on the DFA size bound does not necessarily refute a possibility of a more elaborated indexing structure of size _O_(|_T_|).<tbc>

• One may consider another generalization of the LCS problem for _f_-segmental subsequences, where we are interested in the length of a longest common _f_-segmental subsequences, i.e., the length of longest elements of \(SubSeq^{\le f}(T_1)\cap SubSeq^{\le f}(T_2)\). This is a different problem from the one the literature and this paper have discussed. For example, `abc` is a 2-segmental subsequence of both _T_<sub>1</sub>=`abac` and _T_<sub>2</sub>=`acbc`, while they have different witness segmentations (`ab`,`c`) and (`a`,`bc`). A naive dynamic programming algorithm is possible for this problem (Appendix A), but is it possible to design a more efficient algorithm that runs fast when the solution is big enough like our algorithm for SegLCS?
